questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'If I ______ you, I would accept the job offer without hesitating.'
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.feedback: With the bare present in the 'if' clause the result would need 'will', as in 'I will accept'. It cannot be paired with 'would'.
'If I were you' is the standard second conditional, using 'were' for every person and 'would' plus infinitive in the result clause.
'Had been' places the condition in the past perfect, which is the third conditional and would need 'would have accepted'.
'If I will be' is not a grammatical conditional clause. The 'if' clause of a conditional never carries 'will' as its main verb.

questions.explanation: 'If I were you' belongs to the second conditional and uses 'were' for every person. The result clause takes 'would' plus a bare infinitive, never a past participle.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What kind of conditional is the sentence 'If she had studied harder, she would have passed the exam'?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.feedback: A first conditional describes a real possibility in the future and pairs 'if' plus present with 'will' plus infinitive.
A second conditional pairs an unreal condition with a present result in 'would' plus infinitive, and here the result is in the past.
A third conditional describes an unreal past with 'had' plus participle in the 'if' clause and 'would have' plus participle in the result.
A zero conditional states a general truth and keeps the present in both halves, as in 'If I am tired, I sleep early'.

questions.explanation: The third conditional describes an unreal past. The 'if' clause uses the past perfect and the result clause uses 'would have' plus a past participle.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'If she had taken a taxi, she would not have missed the flight.' Why does the result use 'would not have missed' rather than 'will miss'?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: Because the sentence describes a general rule
options.feedback: A general rule keeps the present in both halves. This sentence reports one specific situation that never happened.
The choice of tense does not depend on whether a verb is regular. The structure of the conditional decides it.

options.text: Because the speaker does not know the facts
options.feedback: The speaker already presents the situation as imagined, since 'would not have' marks an event that failed to occur.

options.text: Because the third conditional places the result in an unreal past
options.feedback: 'Would not have' plus the participle moves the result into the past, matching the unreal past condition in the 'if' clause.

questions.explanation: 'Would have' plus a participle moves the result into the past. That is what makes the whole sentence describe an event that never happened, not a present situation.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which structure forms a correct second conditional?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.text: If + past simple, would + bare infinitive
options.feedback: This is the second conditional pattern: an unreal condition in the past simple produces a present result with 'would'.

options.text: If + present simple, will + bare infinitive
options.feedback: That is the first conditional, which describes a real and probable situation rather than an unreal one.

options.text: If + past perfect, would + bare infinitive
options.feedback: Mixing the past perfect with 'would' plus infinitive breaks the pattern; the past perfect belongs to the third conditional.

options.text: If + past simple, would have + past participle
options.feedback: Adding 'have' plus a participle turns this into a third conditional about the past, not a second one.

questions.explanation: The second conditional pairs the past simple in the 'if' clause with 'would' plus a bare infinitive in the result clause. Every other option mixes two different patterns.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses the third conditional in the negative?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: If I hadn't taken the bus, I wouldn't be late.
options.feedback: 'Wouldn't be late' points to the present, so this mixes a past condition with a present result instead of staying in the past.

options.text: If I hadn't taken the bus, I wouldn't have been late.
options.feedback: Both halves use the past perfect and 'would have', so the sentence stays inside one unreal past frame.

options.text: If I don't take the bus, I won't be late.
options.feedback: This is a first conditional about a real future situation, and it contains neither the past perfect nor 'would have'.

options.text: If I hadn't taken the bus, I wasn't late.
options.feedback: The result clause would need the inverted 'would have' plus a participle; the simple past 'was' cannot carry a third conditional.

questions.explanation: A third conditional in the negative keeps the same past frame in both halves: the past perfect in the 'if' clause and 'would have' plus a participle in the result clause.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'If I ______ enough sleep before the exam, I would have remembered half the vocabulary.'
questions.context: English class in Soyapango, SV.

options.feedback: The third conditional needs the past perfect in the 'if' clause and 'would have' plus a participle in the result, so 'had slept' is the only match.
'Will have' points to the future, but 'would have' in the result clause marks a result that never happened in the past.
Putting 'would' in the 'if' clause reverses the structure of the conditional and makes the sentence ungrammatical here.
'If I have' is the bare present, which would need a present result such as 'I will pass'. With 'would have' the condition must be past.

questions.explanation: A third conditional puts the past perfect in the 'if' clause and 'would have' plus a past participle in the result clause. The two halves must share the same past time frame.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What kind of conditional is the sentence 'If I had a car, I would drive to school'?
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.feedback: A first conditional describes a real possibility in the future with 'if' plus present and 'will' plus infinitive, which this sentence does not do.
The second conditional pairs an unreal condition in the past with a present result in 'would' plus infinitive, exactly as this sentence does.
A third conditional describes a result that failed to happen in the past and needs 'would have' plus a participle, which is absent here.
A zero conditional states a general truth and always uses the present in both halves, as in 'If I am tired, I sleep early'.

questions.explanation: The second conditional describes an unreal or hypothetical situation in the present: 'If' plus past simple, followed by 'would' plus a bare infinitive in the result clause.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'If he had taken the earlier bus, he would not have missed the interview.' Why is 'had taken' in the past perfect?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.text: Because the interview is still happening
options.feedback: The interview belongs to the past, since he missed it. The choice of tense reflects that finished situation rather than a present event.
The tense has nothing to do with whether the verb is regular. The past perfect is required by the third conditional structure.

options.text: Because the third conditional places an unreal condition in the past
options.feedback: A third conditional sets an unreal condition in the past, so the 'if' clause takes the past perfect to match 'would not have'.

options.text: Because the bus runs in the past tense
options.feedback: A regular verb would be 'took'. The past perfect signals a condition the writer imagines as earlier than the missed interview.

questions.explanation: The past perfect is not a matter of which verb is used. It marks a condition that is imagined as earlier than the result, which is exactly what the third conditional requires.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is a correct third conditional question?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: If you had told me, did I help you?
options.feedback: The result clause needs the inverted 'would' with 'have' plus a participle, not the past auxiliary 'did'.

options.text: If you would tell me, would I help you?
options.feedback: The 'if' clause cannot carry 'would'. In a third conditional it always uses the past perfect.

options.text: If you told me, would I have helped you?
options.feedback: The simple past 'told' would leave the two halves in different time frames, so the structure does not match.

options.text: If you had told me, would I have helped you?
options.feedback: This keeps the past perfect in the 'if' clause and inverts 'would' in the result clause, which is the third conditional question pattern.

questions.explanation: A third conditional question keeps the past perfect in the 'if' clause and inverts the auxiliary 'would' in the result clause, with 'have' plus a participle following it.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'If I ______ the invitation, I would have gone to the concert.'
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.feedback: A third conditional asks for 'had' plus the participle in the 'if' clause so that it matches 'would have gone' in the result clause.
'Would' cannot open the 'if' clause of a conditional. Only the result clause carries 'would have' here.
A bare infinitive would need a present result such as 'I will go'. With 'would have gone' the condition has to be in the past.
'Have lost' is the present perfect and belongs to a present result, as in 'I will go'. It does not match 'would have'.

questions.explanation: A third conditional describes an unreal past, so the 'if' clause needs the past perfect 'had' plus a participle to match 'would have gone' in the main clause.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'If I ______ more time after work, I would learn another language.'
questions.context: English class in Soyapango, SV.

options.feedback: A second conditional describes an unreal past situation with a present result, so the 'if' clause uses the past simple and the main clause uses 'would'.
The future perfect in the 'if' clause belongs to a third conditional about the past, not to this unreal present situation.
Using 'would' in the 'if' clause would reverse the conditional and make the sentence ungrammatical.
The bare present could only work with 'will' or 'can' in the main clause; with 'would' the two halves would not match.

questions.explanation: The second conditional pairs an unreal past condition with the present consequence in 'would'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'If I were you, I would apologise to her.' What kind of condition does 'If I were you' set up?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: A condition that will probably happen
options.feedback: There is no prediction about the future. The clause advises on a hypothetical situation rather than forecasting an event.
The sentence does not claim that the situation was real; 'were' marks it as imagined, which is the opposite of certainty.

options.text: An unreal or imagined condition used to give advice
options.feedback: 'If I were you' imagines the listener's position in order to give advice, so the condition is hypothetical rather than factual.

options.text: A condition about somebody else in the past
options.feedback: The pronoun 'you' refers to the listener in the present, so the clause advises about now and not about the past.

questions.explanation: 'If I were you' imagines a situation that is not the listener's own, and the result clause then advises. The condition is hypothetical rather than real or certain.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'If she ______ harder before the exam, she would have passed it.'
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.feedback: The third conditional needs the past perfect in the 'if' clause and 'would have' plus a past participle in the result clause.
With the simple past in the 'if' clause the sentence would be a mixed structure, but here the main clause clearly refers to an unreal past outcome.
The 'if' clause cannot carry 'would' in this pattern, and a past result requires the past perfect anyway.
The present perfect belongs to the second conditional, where the result is present rather than past.

questions.explanation: The third conditional describes an unreal past: the 'if' clause takes 'had' plus a past participle, and the result clause takes 'would have' plus the same participle.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly mixes a past condition with a present result?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.text: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now
options.feedback: This keeps the unreal past in 'had studied' and gives the consequence in the present with 'would be', which is a mixed conditional.

options.text: If I studied medicine, I would be a doctor now
options.feedback: With the simple past and 'would' this is a plain second conditional, so the condition is read as a general case rather than as a past one.

options.text: If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor
options.feedback: 'Would have been' turns the result into the past, so this is a third conditional rather than a mixed one.

options.text: If I would study medicine, I would be a doctor now
options.feedback: Putting 'would' in the 'if' clause is not allowed in a conditional, so the sentence cannot be correct.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional looks back at an unreal past condition with the past perfect and gives the consequence in the present with 'would' plus a bare infinitive.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'If she ______ harder before the exam, she would have passed it.'
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: 'Would' cannot be used in the 'if' clause. The condition of a third conditional always takes the past perfect.
The past perfect 'had studied' sets the unreal past condition and matches the past result 'would have passed' in the main clause.
The present perfect points to the present, so it cannot match a result that is also expressed with 'would have'.
A bare present would need a present result such as 'she will pass'. Here the result is clearly placed in the past.

questions.explanation: A third conditional pairs the past perfect in the 'if' clause with 'would have' plus a participle in the result clause, so both halves refer to the same unreal past.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'Unless you leave now, you ______ the last bus.'
questions.context: English class in Mejicanos, SV.

options.feedback: 'Unless' is logically 'if not', so the consequence is expected when the negative condition fails to be met.
That outcome would require the positive form of the condition, so the meaning would be the opposite of the intended one.
A second conditional would need an unreal condition in the past, which the present-tense 'leave now' does not provide.
A bare future form cannot follow 'unless' as the consequence without an auxiliary, so the sentence would be ungrammatical.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not', so failing to leave now produces the negative consequence.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'I would never have got the scholarship if the professor ______ me.'
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.feedback: A third conditional about an unreal past requires the negative past perfect in the 'if' clause to match 'would have got'.
The simple past would point to a real decision in the past and would not match the unreal tone of the main clause.
The present in the 'if' clause would give a general rule instead of a single unreal past event.
The future form cannot combine with 'would have' in the result clause, since the two halves must share one time frame.

questions.explanation: The unreal past condition pairs 'had not' with 'would have' plus the participle.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In the sentence 'If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now', what kind of conditional is this?
questions.context: English class in Soyapango, SV.

options.text: A mixed conditional, with a past condition and a present result
options.feedback: The 'if' clause is in the past perfect and the result refers to now, which is the definition of a mixed conditional.

options.text: A first conditional about a probable future event
options.feedback: A first conditional pairs a present condition with a future result, which is not what this sentence does.

options.text: A second conditional with an unreal present situation
options.feedback: The condition here is not present but past, so it is not a plain second conditional.

options.text: A third conditional with an unreal past result
options.feedback: The result refers to the present, so the sentence does not describe an outcome that failed to happen in the past.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional looks back at an unreal past condition and draws a consequence for the present.

questions.statement: Which question forms the third conditional correctly?

options.text: If you had warned me, would I have taken the job?

options.text: If you would warn me, would I have taken the job?
options.feedback: The 'if' clause cannot carry 'would'; the pattern is only allowed in the result clause.

options.text: If you had warned me, did I have taken the job?
options.feedback: The result clause needs 'would have' plus the participle, not the simple past auxiliary 'did'.

options.text: If you warned me, would I have taken the job?
options.feedback: The simple past in the condition would make the two halves refer to different time frames.

questions.explanation: Third conditional questions keep the past perfect in the condition and invert 'would' in the result.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'If I ______ harder, I would not be failing maths now.'
questions.context: English class in Soyapango, SV.

options.feedback: A simple past with 'would' is the second conditional, which sets an unreal condition and draws a consequence for the present.
'Had studied' would place the condition in the past, and the result 'I would not be failing' refers to now, so the two halves would no longer belong to the same pattern.
'Would have studied' describes an unreal past action with no result clause of its own, so it cannot stand in the 'if' clause here.
'Will study' points to the future, but the sentence asks about a present failure that follows from an unreal past condition.

questions.explanation: A second conditional uses the past simple in the 'if' clause with 'would' plus a bare infinitive in the result clause, which is how an unreal condition produces a present consequence.
